marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q001.takeaway: Steroids are derived lipids; fats, oils and waxes are simple lipids.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q001.displayText:
Lipids are classified as simple, complex and derived lipids. Steroids are derived lipids because this group includes lipid products or derivatives such as fatty acids, glycerol, sterols/steroids and fat-soluble vitamins.

By contrast, fats and oils are triacylglycerol-type simple lipids, while waxes are simple esters of fatty acids with long-chain alcohols.

rationales.a: Fats are simple lipids, not derived lipids.
rationales.b: Oils are simple lipids, not derived lipids.
rationales.d: Waxes are simple lipids formed from fatty acids and long-chain alcohols.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q002.takeaway: Triacylglycerols are the major storage form of lipid in humans.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q002.displayText:
Triacylglycerols are the major storage form of lipid in the body. Each molecule consists of glycerol esterified to three fatty acids, allowing energy-dense neutral fat to accumulate efficiently in adipose tissue.

Free fatty acids are important circulating fuels, whereas phospholipids are major membrane lipids and lipoproteins are transport particles.
emphasis: Triacylglycerols are the major storage form of lipid
glycerol esterified to three fatty acids

rationales.a: Free fatty acids are circulating fuels but are not the main stored lipid form.
rationales.c: Phospholipids are major structural components of membranes rather than the principal energy store.
rationales.d: Lipoproteins transport lipids in plasma; they are not the body's storage form of lipid.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q003.takeaway: Linoleic acid is polyunsaturated (18:2), whereas caproic, myristic and palmitic acids are saturated.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q003.displayText:
Linoleic acid is a polyunsaturated fatty acid with two double bonds (18:2), so it is not saturated. Saturated fatty acids contain no carbon–carbon double bonds.

Caproic acid, myristic acid and palmitic acid are saturated fatty acids; oleic acid is a classic monounsaturated fatty acid.
emphasis: Linoleic acid is a polyunsaturated fatty acid
Saturated fatty acids contain no carbon–carbon double bonds

rationales.b: Caproic acid is a saturated fatty acid.
rationales.c: Myristic acid is a saturated fatty acid.
rationales.d: Palmitic acid is a saturated fatty acid.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q004.takeaway: Linoleic acid is a PUFA with two double bonds, not a monounsaturated fatty acid.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q004.displayText:
Monounsaturated fatty acids contain one double bond. Palmitoleic acid, oleic acid and elaidic acid each have a single double bond and therefore fit the monounsaturated category.

Linoleic acid has two double bonds and is a polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA), making it the exception.
emphasis: Monounsaturated fatty acids contain one double bond
Linoleic acid has two double bonds

rationales.a: Palmitoleic acid is monounsaturated, with one double bond.
rationales.b: Oleic acid is a classic monounsaturated fatty acid.
rationales.c: Elaidic acid is the trans isomer of oleic acid and still contains one double bond, so it is monounsaturated.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q005.takeaway: Arachidonic acid is a 20-carbon omega-6 PUFA with four double bonds (20:4).
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q005.displayText:
Arachidonic acid contains four double bonds and is conventionally written as 20:4, n-6. It is an omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid incorporated into membrane phospholipids and is an important precursor for eicosanoids.

The source table shows the progression in common PUFAs: linoleic acid has 2 double bonds, linolenic acid 3, arachidonic acid 4, timnodonic acid 5 and cervonic acid 6. The source molecular-structure figure should be read with this 20:4 identity in mind.

rationales.a: One double bond describes a monounsaturated fatty acid, not arachidonic acid.
rationales.b: Two double bonds characterize linoleic acid rather than arachidonic acid.
rationales.c: Three double bonds characterize linolenic acid rather than arachidonic acid.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q006.takeaway: Omega-3 fatty acids generate a less inflammatory eicosanoid profile and have anti-inflammatory effects.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q006.displayText:
Omega-3 fatty acids, including alpha-linolenic acid, EPA and DHA, are associated with anti-inflammatory effects. Increased omega-3 availability shifts eicosanoid production toward mediators that are generally less inflammatory and less thrombogenic than those derived predominantly from omega-6 arachidonic acid.

Omega-3 fatty acids also lower serum triglycerides, which is another clinically important metabolic effect.

rationales.b: Omega-6 fatty acids include arachidonic-acid precursors and are not the source-keyed anti-inflammatory class here.
rationales.c: Omega-9 fatty acids are monounsaturated fats but are not the class identified by this question for anti-inflammatory activity.
rationales.d: Omega-7 fatty acids are not the source-keyed class associated with the anti-inflammatory eicosanoid shift.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q007.takeaway: The essential fatty acids in humans are linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3).
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q007.displayText:
Linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3) are the two essential fatty acids in humans because humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9 of the fatty-acid chain. They must therefore be supplied in the diet.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q008.takeaway: Essential fatty-acid deficiency causes scaly dermatitis, alopecia and poor wound healing; linoleic acid is essential.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q008.displayText:
This child has essential fatty-acid deficiency caused by fat malabsorption from pancreatic insufficiency. The characteristic findings include dry scaly dermatitis, hair loss and impaired wound healing.

Linoleic acid is an essential omega-6 fatty acid and must be obtained from the diet. Conditions that impair fat absorption, including cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency, increase the risk of deficiency.
emphasis: dry scaly dermatitis, hair loss and impaired wound healing
Linoleic acid is an essential omega-6 fatty acid

rationales.a: Arachidonic acid can be synthesized from linoleic acid and is considered conditionally/semi-essential rather than the primary essential fatty acid tested here.
rationales.b: Oleic acid is a nonessential omega-9 monounsaturated fatty acid that humans can synthesize.
rationales.d: Elaidic acid is a trans monounsaturated fatty acid and is not an essential fatty acid.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q009.takeaway: Partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils can convert cis double bonds to trans configuration, producing trans fatty acids.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH12_Q009.displayText:
Trans fatty acids can be produced during partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils. Around a trans double bond, the carbon chains lie on opposite sides, giving the molecule a straighter configuration than the corresponding cis fatty acid; the source figure illustrates this geometry.

Dietary trans fats adversely affect the lipoprotein profile by increasing LDL cholesterol and lowering HDL cholesterol, which contributes to cardiovascular risk.
emphasis: increasing LDL cholesterol and lowering HDL cholesterol

rationales.a: Eicosanoids are signaling lipids derived from polyunsaturated fatty acids; they are not the characteristic by-product of oil hydrogenation.
rationales.b: Glycerol is the alcohol backbone of triacylglycerols and is not produced as the characteristic hydrogenation by-product.
rationales.c: Cis fatty acids are the natural configuration of many unsaturated fatty acids; partial hydrogenation can isomerize some cis bonds to trans rather than producing cis fat as the by-product.
